title: Grifting 101

jokes.text: Well, the candy has lost its appeal now that I work at the store. You might say becoming a teacher here gave me diabetes.
jokes.setup: Someone says Jeff is 'like a kid in a candy store' about the course catalog
jokes.punchline: Jeff extends the metaphor darkly — working at the candy store killed the joy, and he frames his disillusionment as diabetes
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff cynicism weaponized through an extended metaphor. The pivot from 'candy store' to literal diabetes is a sharp misdirection — the audience expects a wry observation about burnout, not an actual medical condition. Works because it's deeply Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm like a kid in a candy store with this course catalog.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Except the candy store is Greendale, and instead of candy, it's courses, and instead of just getting fat, I literally got diabetes.

jokes.text: Are you always thirsty and fatigued and you have blurry vision and your cuts heal slower? Those are actual diabetes symptoms. That's what the doctor said.
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a glib diabetes metaphor
jokes.punchline: Britta immediately recites actual diabetes symptoms at him, escalating the joke from metaphor to possible genuine diagnosis
jokes.explanation: The joke lands because it weaponizes Britta's earnestness — she takes a metaphor literally and in doing so reveals Jeff might actually have diabetes. The rewatch bonus is real: the callback at 18:44 pays this off. Good structural plant.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you actually have diabetes?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I went to the doctor last week. He said my blood sugar levels are through the roof.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff! Why didn't you tell us?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because I was hoping if I didn't say it out loud, it wouldn't be real. Kind of like how I've been handling everything else in my life.

jokes.text: So, is he treating it? / I asked him the same thing. / What did he say? / He said, make an appointment through his office during business hours.
jokes.setup: Britta asks if Jeff's doctor is treating his possible diabetes
jokes.punchline: Jeff went to the doctor at home — this is his home, his children sleep here — and the doctor told him to make a proper appointment
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical delivery. The reveal that Jeff was bugging a doctor at their home — earning the rebuke to 'make an appointment' — is a great character-specific joke. Only Jeff would corner a doctor socially. The rhythm of the exchange is tight and theatrical.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I went to the doctor's house instead of the office.

jokes.text: This is his home, his children sleep here.
jokes.setup: Jeff is recounting being told to make a proper appointment by a doctor
jokes.punchline: A group member adds the detail that Jeff was at the doctor's house, with children present — horrifying context delivered flatly
jokes.explanation: Five words that recontextualize the whole prior exchange. The economy is exceptional — it doesn't explain, it just drops the horror and moves on. The flat delivery implied here amplifies the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Grifters? Oh, I know all about grifting. I could teach you for $50.

jokes.text: Wait, what do grifters do again? / I got this. I'll tell you for five bucks.
jokes.setup: Someone asks what grifters do
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately grifts for the definition of grifting — meta, quick, perfectly executed
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Structurally flawless: the question creates the perfect setup, and Jeff's response IS the answer (he grifts) while simultaneously being a joke. Maximum economy — six words is the entire punchline. Deeply character-specific to Jeff's opportunism. Quotable standalone line that defines grifting better than any definition could.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I want to learn about grifting.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The movie called 'The Grifters' contains almost no actual grifting.

jokes.text: I've always wanted to learn more about grifting ever since I saw 1990's The Grifters, featuring John Cusack, Anjelica Huston, and almost no grifting.
jokes.setup: The group is excited about a grifting class
jokes.punchline: Abed's encyclopedic film knowledge leads to a deadpan review: a movie called The Grifters contains 'almost no grifting'
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed — the specific citation of year, cast, and deflating critical observation is perfectly him. The joke also foreshadows the episode's theme: grifting movies don't actually show grifting (see The Sting callback later). Nice plant.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: At least the last disappointing class gave us goldfish.

jokes.text: You guys, don't take a grifting class. You're going to get grifted. Even more so than by that oceanography class, only none of you will even get a goldfish, then you're gonna come crying back to me.
jokes.setup: The group wants to take the grifting class; Jeff objects
jokes.punchline: Jeff's prediction is specific and petty — referencing a previous Greendale scam class and predicting the exact emotional arc that will follow
jokes.explanation: The reference to the oceanography class and 'not even a goldfish' is a nice specific Greendale-flavored detail. Rewatch bonus because Jeff is completely right — they do come crying back. The specificity of the goldfish detail saves this from being generic exposition.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You know what your problem is? You're a con man. You con people, you con yourself, and worst of all, you con us into thinking you're going to change.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not fair.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Isn't it? Because next week you'll do something selfish, we'll all be disappointed, and then you'll say something charming and we'll all forgive you. It's a con, Jeff. And we're all suckers for it.

jokes.text: Oh, this is one of those things where Jeff gets jealous of something dumb.
jokes.setup: Jeff is making a big deal of the grifting class
jokes.punchline: Britta names the sitcom trope they're in — 'one of those things' — reducing Jeff's whole arc to a recognizable pattern
jokes.explanation: Very Community — meta-awareness of their own episode structure. Britta naming the trope deflates it while simultaneously confirming it. 'Something dumb' does a lot of work. The show is diagnosing itself out loud, which is brand-appropriate craft.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Even I, who lives in an RV with a fold-down table, can judge Jeff

jokes.text: Jeff's jealous of a grifter. Because he wishes he was still a grifter.
jokes.setup: The group is processing Jeff's objection to the class
jokes.punchline: Abed provides a clinical talking-head narration of Jeff's psychology as if doing a nature documentary
jokes.explanation: Abed's flat analytical narration of Jeff's emotional state is a reliable Community device. The two-sentence structure — observation, then self-evident 'because' explanation — lands as deadpan understatement. Character-specific to Abed's documentary worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Hey, can you cover for me in grifting class?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Cover for you? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'll owe you one. You cover my class, I'll cover yours next week, then you cover my anthropology class the week after, but only on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Then I'll owe you two favors, which you can cash in anytime before the semester ends, but not during midterms. And if I miss class for any reason other than illness or family emergency, the whole deal is void and you get to pick what I wear for a day.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, there's more. You also get a coupon for one free meal at lunch, redeemable only in the cafeteria, and I'll name my firstborn child after you, but only if it's a boy, and only if you approve the middle name. Oh, and high five!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: High five.

jokes.text: That's something even I could mock, and I live in an RV. I'm judging you, and my dinner table folds down from a wall.
jokes.setup: The group is piling on Jeff's jealousy of a grifting professor
jokes.punchline: Elroy establishes his living situation as a credential for mockery — if he, who lives in an RV with a fold-down dinner table, can judge Jeff, the bar is very low
jokes.explanation: Classic Elroy self-deprecation used as a weapon. The specificity of 'dinner table folds down from a wall' elevates this beyond a simple 'even I think you're pathetic' beat. It's precise and visual. The double structure (RV, then dinner table detail) works like a one-two punch.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, if it's a basic class, why do we need briefcases? That doesn't seem very basic.

jokes.text: I say we all take the grifting class together, have a great time, and rub it in Jeff's face! Who's in, and can you cover me? I'll pay you back. I'll get it from your parents.
jokes.setup: Britta rallies the group against Jeff and immediately needs to borrow money
jokes.punchline: Britta's rousing speech immediately collapses into her standard financial dependence on others, and Annie's 'I'll get it from your parents' is a devastating addendum
jokes.explanation: Britta's heroic moment immediately undercut by her chronic poverty is a well-worn but well-executed character beat. What elevates it is Annie's 'I'll get it from your parents' — a cold, specific threat that shows Annie's capability for ruthlessness when motivated.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh wow, extra briefcases? What a shocker.

jokes.text: All right, each student should bring a briefcase. / We're gonna grift with briefcases? / Basic my ass, that's advanced.
jokes.setup: Professor DeSalvo announces the briefcase requirement for 'Basic Grifting'
jokes.punchline: Elroy's immediate reframe: a briefcase makes it 'advanced,' not basic
jokes.explanation: Quick, punchy joke about the absurdity of the class's self-designation. 'Basic my ass' is a solid reactive line. Not deeply crafted but efficiently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: So what exactly are regulation briefcases?

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: You know, I have no idea what they are.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Then why are you selling them?

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Because they're regulation.

jokes.text: I have a few extra briefcases. / Shocker. Are they regulation? / We each need a regulation grifting briefcase. / It's a grift. / What's a regulation briefcase? / I don't know. But they're provided for only $150. / You're being grifted. / Shut up, Jeff.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo introduces the concept of a 'regulation grifting briefcase'
jokes.punchline: Jeff correctly identifies they're being grifted in real time; the group tells him to shut up anyway — establishing the episode's central comic engine
jokes.explanation: This is the structural linchpin of the episode's first act comedy — DeSalvo is visibly grifting them right now, Jeff calls it out clearly and correctly, and the group rejects his accurate warning because of social dynamics. The 'Shocker' on Abed having extra briefcases is a nice sidebar that deepens the gag. The escalating 'What's a regulation briefcase? / I don't know' sequence shows the class as a pure hustle. Rewatch bonus because the audience knows everything Jeff said was true.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Can I borrow some money?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: See? Taken advantage of.

jokes.text: What do you contribute to this group besides negativity? / Guys, watch this, can I borrow $150? / No. / See!
jokes.setup: Annie challenges Jeff on his negativity; Jeff offers to prove a point
jokes.punchline: Jeff asks to borrow $150 (exactly what DeSalvo wants) and when refused, uses their refusal as proof of his point — that they're being irrational about money
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: Jeff uses the same grift mechanic (ask for $150) on the group and when they refuse, the 'See!' reveals they know $150 is too much to give a stranger — but they'll pay DeSalvo anyway. It's a micro-grift that proves his macro-point. Economy is superb — the punchline is one word. This is the kind of internally logical comedy that elevates Community above average sitcoms.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Look, I have a payment plan. I'll pay you back in installments.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Five dollars a month for the next... *counts on fingers* ...eight hundred years. Your great-great-grandchildren will thank me.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: And frankly, you should be grateful. Most people wouldn't even offer that much. Also, you're bad parents.

jokes.text: Now who's gonna come with me and show this guy what's up? / I'll pay you back. I'll get it from your parents. / Tell them I spit on their wealth and thank you.
jokes.setup: Britta rallies the group while still needing money from Annie, who threatens to get it from Britta's parents
jokes.punchline: Britta's response to her parents being leveraged: 'Tell them I spit on their wealth and thank you' — she's simultaneously defiant and grateful in one sentence
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Britta. The contradiction of spitting on wealth while gratefully accepting it encapsulates her entire character arc across six seasons. 'Spit on their wealth AND thank you' in one breath is high-quotability character comedy. The character integration score is near-perfect — this joke could ONLY be Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Professor DeSalvo
dialogue.line: I'm Professor DeSalvo, and I'm a grifter. I've taught at 47 different colleges under various aliases like Dirk Studmeyer, Buck Thunderpants, and my personal favorite, Blast Hardcheese.

jokes.text: My name is Professor Roger DeSalvo, for the time being.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo introduces himself as a grifting professor
jokes.punchline: 'For the time being' — immediately signaling his name is provisional, which is simultaneously an in-character grifter detail and a wink to the audience
jokes.explanation: Economical character establishment. Four words ('for the time being') do the entire comedic job of signaling DeSalvo's nature without overexplaining. Good comic timing on the qualifier.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: My name is... uh... Jeff Winger.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: No wait, it's Jeff... Goulash.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm Jeff Biscotto.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Hold on, Jeff Spaghetti-O.

jokes.text: For I use many a pseudonym, such as Jeff Goulash, Philip Switch, or Baz Ravish.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo explains he uses many pseudonyms
jokes.punchline: The names themselves — Jeff Goulash, Philip Switch, Baz Ravish — are absurdist comedy gold, escalating in ridiculousness
jokes.explanation: The names are specifically crafted to be absurdly non-grifter-like: 'Jeff Goulash' sounds like a food complaint, 'Philip Switch' like a minor electrical component, 'Baz Ravish' like an aggressive perfume. The escalation toward 'Baz Ravish' — which sounds vaguely threatening and vaguely sexy — is the peak. High originality and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: I meant to do that. It's a classic grifting technique—make them think you're incompetent so they lower their guard.

jokes.text: Now which one of you thinks I did that on purpose? / [group reacts] / Exactly, you think you've seen me fail.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo apparently does something awkward or stumbles on his entrance, then addresses the class
jokes.punchline: He reveals the apparent mistake was deliberate — a meta-lesson about grifting that is itself potentially a grift about whether the mistake was real
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony setup — was it deliberate? The audience can't know, which is the joke. DeSalvo immediately layers the grift meta-commentary into his first classroom moment. Rewatch bonus because it establishes DeSalvo's unreliable nature early.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Pass it! Pass it! PASS IT!

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Faster! FASTER! We need to move NOW!

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: GO GO GO! This is critical! MOVE!

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: We've got 40 minutes.

jokes.text: Pass them like your sister's dying, and continue that for about 40 minutes.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo escalates instructions for briefcase passing with increasingly dramatic urgency
jokes.punchline: 'Pass them like your sister's dying' — an absurdly dark motivational instruction, followed by 'and continue that for about 40 minutes' which deflates the drama into the mundane
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The dark urgency ('your sister's dying') followed immediately by the banal bureaucracy ('for about 40 minutes') is a perfect comedic whiplash. It's also a micro-grift — the emotional manipulation is pointless because it's just briefcase passing. Highly quotable and original. This is the kind of absurdist escalation Community excels at.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Your real name is Annie Kim? That's a terrible name.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, from now on, call me Analise Risotto Pinot Grigio.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Actually, never mind. I'm Annie.

jokes.text: What's your name, my love? / Annie Edison. / That sounds like a real name, not the name of a grifter and therefore, not a teacher.
jokes.setup: Annie asks a reasonable question about the curriculum
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo dismisses her by critiquing her name as 'too real' — a grifter professor who demands students have fake names
jokes.explanation: Good inverted logic — in grifting class, 'real name' is an insult. The professor's authority is built on the reversal of normal classroom values. Funny and character-establishing for DeSalvo.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Wait, you're telling me DeSalvo tried to sell 'extra believable socks'?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: How is that even a product?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: I thought I was getting a deal!

jokes.text: My name is Slick Pockets Tucker. / No, it's not. / That's correct. I was just wondering what the next lesson will be.
jokes.setup: Annie attempts to adopt a grifter alias to satisfy DeSalvo
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo immediately sees through it; Annie backtracks with perfect earnestness — 'That's correct. I was just wondering...'
jokes.explanation: Very Annie — she chooses an objectively terrible grifter name ('Slick Pockets Tucker'), gets caught immediately, and her graceful retreat to 'That's correct, I was just wondering' is both a good save and an admission of failure. High character integration: this is specifically the Annie Type-A overcorrection.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone sit down. I want to hear this, but I need to get comfortable first.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, can you grab me that pillow? And maybe adjust the lighting? I've been waiting for this moment my entire life.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff, we just need to tell you that you were—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Ah ah ah. Not yet. Is anyone recording this? We should document this.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, now I'm ready. Go ahead.

jokes.text: Oh no, grifters. I better watch my french fries unless, counterfeit?
jokes.setup: The grifting class students walk by Jeff with their briefcases, visibly performing 'grifter' energy
jokes.punchline: Jeff's mock-paranoia — 'counterfeit french fries' — reduces their theatrical menace to absurdity
jokes.explanation: Jeff doing theatrically bad fake-fear is a solid comedic beat. The 'counterfeit french fries' escalation is absurdist and funny. His mockery lands because the group IS playing grifter dress-up with zero substance.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I appreciate the apologies, but I have to be honest with you guys. I'm not actually hurt. I'm just lazy and I like having an excuse to do nothing.

jokes.text: Where'd you learn to do that? / We didn't learn anything. That class is... A rip off? / Hm, what's another word for that?
jokes.setup: Jeff watches the group do briefcase tricks; they admit the class taught them nothing
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'What's another word for that?' forcing them to say 'grift' — completing the circle of his original warning
jokes.explanation: Jeff engineering the moment where they have to admit he was right, without saying it directly — just asking 'what's another word for that?' — is economical and smart. Satisfying callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You're as lazy as DeSalvo.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: DeSalvo? The Boston Strangler?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, I mean in terms of laziness. He never left his apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's because he was in prison.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, you're doing the reverse. You're leaving your apartment but accomplishing nothing, which is like reverse pissing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I don't know, I'm making it up as I go.

jokes.text: And, he kept trying to sell us stuff. Briefcase swapping talcum for grifter's palm, briefcase hinge oil for silence switcheroos, and something called extra believable socks.
jokes.setup: The group recounts how DeSalvo kept upselling them in class
jokes.punchline: The list of upsell items escalates beautifully: talcum powder has logic, hinge oil has marginal logic, then 'extra believable socks' has no logic at all
jokes.explanation: 'Extra believable socks' is an outstanding absurdist invention. The escalation from logical grifter accessories to 'socks that make you believable' is a perfect rule-of-three with the third term being completely unhinged. The concept of socks conferring believability is delightfully specific nonsense. High quotability — 'extra believable socks' is a standalone joke that could leave the episode and still be funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm Jeff Winger. I'm a lawyer. Well, I was a lawyer. Well, I'm still a lawyer, I just can't practice law anymore. But I'm very tolerant of other cultures and religions. I have a Latina girlfriend. Well, I did. We broke up. But the point is, I'm not racist. I'm just saying, you know, some people are different, and that's okay. As long as they stay in their own neighborhoods.

jokes.text: Those are actually half off, I kind of feel like I grifted him.
jokes.setup: The group complains about DeSalvo's upselling of grifter supplies
jokes.punchline: Abed reveals he bought the socks but got a discount — and frames that as HIM grifting DeSalvo
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed — he genuinely believes getting 50% off nonsense socks is a counter-grift. The deadpan sincerity makes it work. Also quietly funny that he bought the socks at all.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is my desk.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And this is DeSalvo's desk. It's the one that's empty because DeSalvo doesn't exist.

jokes.text: So in a sense, what happened is you took a class about grifting. / Aaaaaannnnnd... Jeff, you really need us to say it? / You were... Eh, whoa, whoa, yeah I need you to say it. Let me just get settled. Okay go. / You were right.
jokes.setup: The group has to admit Jeff was right
jokes.punchline: Jeff theatrically demanding they say it, physically settling in, then commanding 'okay go' — turning their capitulation into a performance he's directing
jokes.explanation: Jeff's narcissistic need to have his vindication performed for him — 'Let me just get settled. Okay go.' — is peak Jeff character comedy. The audience knows exactly what he's doing and enjoys watching him do it unironically. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Grifting isn't lying, it's theater. It's like... it's like a magician pulling a rabbit out of a hat.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Except the rabbit is money, and the hat is someone's trust, and the magician is me.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Which is basically just lying.

jokes.text: Well, you live and you learn, guys. / Well, you live anyway.
jokes.setup: Jeff offers a compassionate-sounding platitude after being vindicated
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts it — 'Well, you live anyway' — implying they haven't learned and probably won't
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The setup ('you live and you learn') is instantly recognizable as a kindness platitude. The punchline ('you live anyway') strips out the 'learn' half, delivering maximum cynicism in minimum words. Perfect Jeff — generous enough to let them have the moment, contemptuous enough to take it back. Economy score is 9 because three words do enormous comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm not just a lawyer. I'm the best lawyer in this city.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Oh please. I'm not just a cop. I'm a decorated officer who's solved more cases than you've won arguments.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well I'm not just decorated — I'm a legend. People write dissertations about my cross-examinations.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: That's nothing. I'm not just a legend — I'm an institution. They named a wing of the precinct after me.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Fine. I'm not just an institution — I'm a force of nature. I bend the laws of physics with my closing statements.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Well I'm not just a force of nature — I'm a cosmic entity. Planets realign when I enter a room.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You want to know what I am? I'm God.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: ...I'm also God.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We can't both be God.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Then I guess we're going to have to fight about it.

jokes.text: My feelings are fine. I'm just very lazy, and you gave me an excuse to do nothing. I'm not just gonna throw that away.
jokes.setup: The group apologizes for hurting Jeff's feelings when refusing to listen to him
jokes.punchline: Jeff corrects them: it's not about feelings — he's lazy, they gave him an excuse to abstain, and he intends to hold onto that excuse
jokes.explanation: Deep Jeff character comedy. He's not hurt — he's weaponizing his laziness strategically and is completely transparent about it. 'I'm not just gonna throw that away' treats his excuse as a physical object worth protecting. Very high character integration: this joke exists only because of Jeff's specific psychology.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what, DeSalvo? I'm done with your—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I love you.

jokes.text: He's even lazier than you. Doesn't your species consider that a challenge? Shouldn't you be on some kind of reverse pissing contest to determine who's laziest?
jokes.setup: Jeff refuses to help grift DeSalvo because he's too lazy
jokes.punchline: Annie frames Jeff's laziness as a species characteristic with its own competitive hierarchy — a 'reverse pissing contest for laziness'
jokes.explanation: 'Your species' frames Jeff's laziness as a biological category, which is a funny anthropological distancing. 'Reverse pissing contest' is an unexpected compound image. Annie weaponizing Jeff's ego against his laziness is good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's actually getting easier.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Why? What changed?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, we've dropped it so many times that the handle broke off, so now it's just a box. And boxes are easier to pass than briefcases.

jokes.text: Wait, is that where you suck it back up in your? / I'm sorry, I've only ever done it the other way. / You mean peeing? / No, I mean in the back.
jokes.setup: Annie mentions a 'reverse pissing contest'
jokes.punchline: Jeff takes the metaphor literally and asks if 'reverse' means physically sucking it back in — then clarifies he does it 'in the back,' whatever that means
jokes.explanation: Classic Community digression — metaphor taken grotesquely literal. 'No, I mean in the back' is a pure absurdist payoff that doesn't explain anything, which is exactly right. The confusion it creates is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Stop using that word! You're grifting my brain!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I asked for coffee this morning and I said, 'Can you grift me a latte?'

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: My mother called and I told her to stop grifting around!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm losing my mind! I can't stop grifting!

jokes.text: He hasn't done anything to me. In fact, he sounds like a pretty good guy. I bet we'd get along.
jokes.setup: The group wants Jeff to help them get revenge on DeSalvo
jokes.punchline: Jeff's sudden reversal — DeSalvo sounds like 'a pretty good guy,' implying Jeff identifies with him as a fellow grifter/con man
jokes.explanation: Setup for the Jeff/DeSalvo dynamic — Jeff's recognition of a kindred spirit foreshadows their contentious office relationship. The quick pivot from righteous to suddenly sympathetic is a character-specific joke about Jeff's moral flexibility.

dialogue.speaker: Telegram Man
dialogue.line: Telegram for you, sir.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: What's it say?

dialogue.speaker: Telegram Man
dialogue.line: Greetings. I am a Nigerian prince. I have inherited a large sum of money and need your help to transfer it. All I need is your banking information and a small processing fee.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: A Nigerian prince email scam... delivered as a telegram?

dialogue.speaker: Telegram Man
dialogue.line: Those are the terms of the will, sir.

jokes.text: Well, I was the guy with a full bottle of scotch and a high tolerance for foreigners.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo asks who Jeff is as they meet in the faculty lounge
jokes.punchline: Jeff introduces himself not by name or role but by his two current qualities: scotch and xenophilic tolerance
jokes.explanation: 'High tolerance for foreigners' is a funny, slightly uncomfortable self-description — it's technically a compliment but phrased as if tolerating foreigners is a feat. Jeff introducing himself through his coping mechanisms rather than his identity is perfectly in-character.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: This is the Jim Belushi of grift — ubiquitous but not respected.

jokes.text: That would be your desk. If you need a mnemonic device, it's the one without someone else's stuff all over it.
jokes.setup: Jeff and DeSalvo are sharing an office; Jeff shows DeSalvo his desk
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'mnemonic device' — the desk that doesn't have his stuff on it — is a condescending way of describing an empty desk
jokes.explanation: Jeff's condescension is channeled through unnecessary pseudo-helpfulness ('mnemonic device'). The joke is in the word 'mnemonic' — it implies DeSalvo needs a memory trick to identify an empty desk. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The Slovenian Switch, the Hungarian Hustle, the Carrot Top Catastrophe...

jokes.text: Grifting people by selling them grifting lessons? It's genius, but I called it.
jokes.setup: Jeff acknowledges DeSalvo's grift is brilliant
jokes.punchline: He immediately stakes a prior claim — 'but I called it' — as if identifying a grift equals performing it
jokes.explanation: Jeff's narcissism is the joke — he thinks predicting the grift makes him a co-author of it. Decent but not the sharpest Jeff ego beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Hey, look at this lottery ticket I found!

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: What lottery ticket? There is no lottery ticket. I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dude, there's clearly a lottery ticket right there.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: No, no, no. You're confused. There never was a ticket. And there was no telegram man either.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Nobody said anything about a telegram man.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Exactly! Because he doesn't exist!

jokes.text: I worked at one of the top law firms in the city as a lawyer, but guess what. I'm not a lawyer. / Well, I think you're talking about lying. Grifting happens to be an art form. / The art of lying. / Let's not get high-handed.
jokes.setup: Jeff claims kinship with DeSalvo by confessing he was a fake lawyer
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo dismisses Jeff's fraud as mere 'lying' — beneath grifting — establishing their ideological dispute
jokes.explanation: The grifting vs. lying debate is the comedic core of the Jeff/DeSalvo dynamic. 'The art of lying' / 'Let's not get high-handed' is a sharp little exchange. Jeff getting snobbish about grifting is funny given his background.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: I'm warning you, I will hurt you!

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: I will actually hurt you! Don't think I won't!

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Wait, am I being too aggressive? Is that too much?

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Nobody respects me, do they? They think I'm soft.

jokes.text: So, like a string is a sweater? Like, paint is the Sistine Chapel? Sure, grifting includes lying, but only a liar would call grifting lying.
jokes.setup: Jeff says grifting is just lying
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo makes an analogy argument that escalates to the Sistine Chapel, then concludes with 'only a liar would call grifting lying' — a circular argument that's self-aware
jokes.explanation: 'Only a liar would call grifting lying' is a beautifully circular, self-undermining argument delivered with complete sincerity. The escalation from string/sweater to Sistine Chapel sets up the logical framework, then the punchline turns it on itself. High quotability — this is a memorable formulation.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Presumably walks into something while walking backwards

jokes.text: And, only a delusional hobo would glorify stealing. / Really? Did you say something that wasn't true there? / Maybe we should phone the museum.
jokes.setup: Jeff calls DeSalvo a 'delusional hobo' for glorifying grifting
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo fires back implying Jeff lied ('Did you say something that wasn't true?'), then suggests calling the museum — continuing the Sistine Chapel metaphor as a threat
jokes.explanation: 'Maybe we should phone the museum' is a perfect callback escalation — DeSalvo is threatening to 'report' Jeff's lie the way you'd report art theft. The absurdity of using the Sistine Chapel metaphor as a rhetorical weapon is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Jeff is obsessed with DeSalvo.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Oh, you two are together? That's impressive.

jokes.text: I was on your side. / You're an ass. / Well, you're a craftless, artless thug. / And, I'm God's paintbrush. / No, I am God, which pretty much makes me better than you.
jokes.setup: Jeff and DeSalvo are competing in increasingly grandiose insults
jokes.punchline: Jeff's escalation to 'I am God' — one-upping DeSalvo's 'paintbrush' claim by being the entire deity
jokes.explanation: The Sistine Chapel metaphor has now fully escalated to competing claims of divinity. The escalation logic is clean — paintbrush leads to God — and Jeff's flat 'which pretty much makes me better than you' is a satisfying deflation after the grandiosity.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you don't have a plan, do you?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Of course I have a plan.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No you don't. None of us do. We're just making this up as we go along.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not true.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff, we're in a TV show. The writers don't even know what happens next week.

jokes.text: Let's agree to disagree. It's not important. / Oh, okay. / So, you can lie. / Yeah, you liar.
jokes.setup: Jeff proposes a truce
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo immediately uses Jeff's truce as proof he lied ('it IS important'), and Jeff just agrees: 'Yeah, you liar'
jokes.explanation: Quick and tidy — the truce is itself caught as a lie within seconds, and Jeff's 'Yeah, you liar' self-applies. Good economy but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: When could I have planned a grift?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You had a lot of time to admit you had no plan.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, I didn't want to look stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Too late.

jokes.text: I wanna speak to you, you son of a bitch. / What? / I love you. / Oh. / I do too. / Good. / Hm.
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts DeSalvo aggressively — 'you son of a bitch'
jokes.punchline: The aggressive opening resolves into a mutual declaration of professional love/respect — 'I love you' / 'I do too'
jokes.explanation: Outstanding misdirection. The 'you son of a bitch' setup promises conflict; the 'I love you' punchline delivers kinship. The subsequent 'Good. / Hm.' exchange — both men accepting this awkward mutual affection with minimal words — is perfectly economical. This is a great comedic moment: the two most cynical characters in the scene acknowledge genuine connection in the least romantic way possible.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Well, if we're having children, they'll need to learn the con game early. I'm thinking by age five, they're running basic short cons at the playground. By ten, they're into the long game.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed, you can't marry a movie.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's exactly what they said about Cher and her boyfriend in Clueless, and look how that turned out.

jokes.text: Why are you guys still doing that? / Well, it was homework, and we're getting better, right? / Or, the friction has gradually melted the handle to fit into our palms.
jokes.setup: The group is still compulsively passing briefcases after the class is revealed as a grift
jokes.punchline: Abed's clinical alternative explanation — the handles melted to their hands from friction — delivered as a neutral hypothesis
jokes.explanation: Abed's physics hypothesis is delivered as a genuine alternative to Annie's optimism, which is funnier than a joke. The idea that they've been doing it so long the handles MERGED with their hands suggests they're in a Pavlovian loop they can't escape — which is also the episode's satirical point about the class.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I need to win. I need to win so badly. It's not about the school, or the team, or any of that. I just... I need people to think I'm good at something. I need to be the best. Because if I'm not winning, what am I? I'm just a guy. A regular guy. And I can't... I can't be that.

jokes.text: The next person who says grift is gonna grift! / My god, now it's replacing other words.
jokes.setup: The group has been saying 'grift' so much it's saturating their vocabulary
jokes.punchline: Britta accidentally uses 'grift' as a threat-verb (instead of 'get it'), and Jeff notes it's now replacing other words — the word has become infectious
jokes.explanation: Britta accidentally inventing a new use of 'grift' as a threat, then Jeff's horror that the word has become viral language, is excellent meta-comedy. 'Now it's replacing other words' is a great observation joke about how certain words colonize discourse. Rewatch bonus because it sets up the later 'grift, grift, grift, grift' chant payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I had a dream last night where everything was dialogue from The Sting. I was walking through a grocery store and the checkout guy was like, 'You know, kid, in this life you gotta learn to appreciate the con within the con.' And I just wanted cereal.

jokes.text: Why are you cheering? He could be saying anything. / Grift!
jokes.setup: Jeff says 'I'm in' and the group cheers before hearing his plan
jokes.punchline: Jeff correctly notes they cheered before knowing what he said; Britta responds with 'Grift!' — confirming the word has fully replaced rational thought
jokes.explanation: The 'Grift!' as a one-word battle cry is a satisfying payoff to the word-replacement gag. Jeff's sharp observation that they cheered before knowing his plan is correct and funny, and Britta's 'Grift!' in response demonstrates exactly what he was warning about.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: What are you doing hiding in here watching movies? You look like a bunch of gypsies.

jokes.text: This isn't real money, it's just cut up newspaper. But it weighs the same, costs five dollars a piece. You'll be using ten.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo introduces 'actual fake money' for the next lesson
jokes.punchline: He explains it's newspaper cut to size, charges $5 per sheet, and they need ten — an escalating grift within the grift revealed mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: Classic DeSalvo escalation — fake money (newspaper) sells for $5/sheet while he simultaneously reveals they need ten. The confidence of the grift, the mundane detail ('it weighs the same'), and the immediate $50 cost reveal is structurally clean.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: You're like a... you're like a... I got nothing. You know what? Oscar Wilde once said, 'Some people are like clouds. When they disappear, it's a beautiful day.'

jokes.text: Telegram for Elroy Patashnik. / I'm Patashnik. / Telegram, sir. / Oh, my God. My Aunt Baba died on vacation while in Africa. Aw. / But she left me a million dollars, but the African government wants to seize the funds. / Class dismissed. Not you.
jokes.setup: A telegram man arrives mid-class with a telegram for Elroy
jokes.punchline: The telegram is a textbook 419 advance fee fraud ('Nigerian prince' scheme) — DeSalvo immediately dismisses class but keeps Elroy, suggesting he's going to pursue it seriously
jokes.explanation: The 419 scam delivered in person via telegram man is a great comedic choice — it's simultaneously the most recognizable internet scam and the most analog possible delivery method. 'Class dismissed. Not you.' is a great button — DeSalvo momentarily dropping all pretense to pursue a grift mid-class. High rewatch value because this sets up the later fake-bait/real-bait discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your fighting style is terrible.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: At least I'm from somewhere real.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're from New Jersey, DeSalvo.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Are you out of your mind? / What? The African telegram. / The Jim Belushi of grift? Are you trying to grift me? / I'll cut you in for fourteen grand.
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts DeSalvo about the African telegram grift
jokes.punchline: 'The Jim Belushi of grift' — implying it's the cheap, embarrassing version of the real thing
jokes.explanation: 'The Jim Belushi of grift' is a devastating and original formulation. Jim Belushi as cultural shorthand for 'the inferior, embarrassing version of something that used to be respected' is a specific, mean, and perfectly calibrated reference. High originality — this is a novel insult construction that doubles as cultural commentary. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, is that real blood?

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: It's corn syrup and food coloring.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh thank God. My diabetes prevents me from tasting fake blood.

jokes.text: One more thing. / Nice try twice. / Twice? The fake grift within the grift, or the double bean, if you like.
jokes.setup: Jeff is leaving DeSalvo's office when DeSalvo calls him back ('one more thing')
jokes.punchline: Jeff catches it as 'nice try twice' — the 'one more thing' is itself a grift attempt; DeSalvo names it 'the double bean'
jokes.explanation: Jeff recognizing 'one more thing' as a grift attempt ('nice try twice') is sharp comedy-of-competence. 'The double bean' as DeSalvo's technical term for a grift-within-a-grift is a funny invented piece of jargon. The confidence with which he names it validates that it was indeed a technique.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm sorry about all this.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Sorry? You're sorry? You're a spineless, narcissistic con artist.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: You're a parasite on society, a waste of human potential.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: And frankly, this entire school is a monument to mediocrity and failure.

jokes.text: I'm gonna mention a name and however you react, I'll know the truth. / Jeff Winger, that's the one! / Jeff Winger? What with the, who? / That's the one. Out you go. Say hi to him.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo threatens to read Jeff's reaction to a name to deduce the truth
jokes.punchline: Jeff's reaction to his own name ('What with the, who?') is comically terrible as a misdirection attempt — DeSalvo sees through it immediately
jokes.explanation: Jeff, supposedly the grifter, produces the worst possible deflection — 'What with the, who?' — which is barely even a sentence. For a character who considers himself a skilled liar, this is a great undercutting joke. The rhythm of DeSalvo's 'That's the one. Out you go. Say hi to him.' is perfect deadpan authority.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: Britta, you're expelled.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: I don't know, but statistically speaking, it's probably your fault.

jokes.text: By the way, Jeff Winger, nice try thrice.
jokes.setup: Jeff leaves DeSalvo's office after the double bean sequence
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo calls after him — 'nice try thrice' — meaning Jeff's exit itself was a grift attempt, and DeSalvo caught it
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous comedic payload. 'Nice try thrice' completes the sequence (once/twice/thrice) while also catching a third grift attempt the audience may not have even identified. The escalating counter-count — once, twice, thrice — is structurally elegant and highly quotable. Economy score of 9: three words do the full job.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta... she's the heart of this group. She cares about everyone, she's selfless, she—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, no... she joined the study group to get over some guy, right?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Um... I mean, that's... that's not... she's still...

jokes.text: Hey, how was grifting class? Did you teach some advanced grifting techniques only you could understand? The Brown Betty? The Texas oil baby? The reverse Jim Gaffigan?
jokes.setup: Annie asks Jeff mockingly about his interaction with DeSalvo
jokes.punchline: The invented grift names escalate absurdly: 'The Brown Betty' (old-fashioned pastry), 'The Texas oil baby' (evocative but bizarre), 'The reverse Jim Gaffigan' (a comedian, reversed, as a grift technique)
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. The invented grift names follow a perfect escalation: 'Brown Betty' sounds vaguely plausible, 'Texas oil baby' is regionally evocative but nonsensical, and 'The reverse Jim Gaffigan' is completely unhinged — a technique named after a comedian, but reversed. The specificity of choosing Jim Gaffigan (a mild, clean comedian) as a grift archetype is inspired nonsense. High originality and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta is essential to this group. She's the moral compass, the voice of reason—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Without her, we'd all just be sleeping with each other!

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Yeah, that would be bad.

jokes.text: Well, I wouldn't teach the African telegram. Since I'm not a hack. And also, since the Internet.
jokes.setup: Annie's mocking list of grift techniques leads Jeff to respond about the African telegram
jokes.punchline: Jeff's two-reason dismissal: artistic principle ('not a hack') AND practical obsolescence ('the Internet')
jokes.explanation: 'And also, since the Internet' is a perfect economic addendum — the matter-of-fact acknowledgment that the grift is simply obsolete, delivered as an afterthought to the more self-aggrandizing 'not a hack' reason. The two-reason structure creates a funny deflation on the second.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, Britta may not be perfect, but she's a good person. She deserves our support.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And if you can't see that, then you're missing the entire character arc of this season. This is peak storytelling. We're in act two of a three-act structure, and Britta's redemption is the B-plot that ties everything together.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So either you're with us, or you're getting a spinoff and nobody's watching it.

jokes.text: Sir, you. That guy left his lottery ticket on the table. / That was the telegram man. / No, it wasn't. / I mean what telegram? / Exactly. What telegram? Because the Internet, you know?
jokes.setup: DeSalvo points out a lottery ticket left by the 'telegram man'
jokes.punchline: Jeff catches it as a grift immediately, and DeSalvo's recovery ('I mean what telegram?') fails; Jeff's 'Because the Internet, you know?' echoes his own earlier line back at DeSalvo as proof
jokes.explanation: Jeff catches a new grift attempt and mirrors DeSalvo's telegrams back at him using his own earlier 'since the Internet' quip. The callback gives Jeff a moment of genuine competence and the exchange has a pleasing game-like quality.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You know, Miss Perry, I have to say - for someone who just got expelled, you showed remarkable cunning in that grift. Have you considered a career in politics?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, are you complimenting me right now?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm saying you have a gift. It would be a shame to waste it.

jokes.text: I'm gonna grift you. I'm gonna grift your ass. Or is that the grift? None of it is a grift! It's all nonsense!
jokes.setup: Jeff and DeSalvo are spiraling into mutual accusations of grifting
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'None of it is a grift! It's all nonsense!' is a moment of genuine meta-clarity — the whole framework is collapsing under its own paranoid logic
jokes.explanation: Jeff's breakdown moment where he denounces the entire framework is funny precisely because he's the one who was complaining about grifting from the start. His frustration that even he can't tell what's real anymore is a satisfying thematic and comedic payoff.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: I'm a lucky grifter, yeah that's what they call me

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Lucky grifter, I can talk my way out of anything

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Well actually, I'm more than a grifter, I'm a con man

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Con man, I've conned presidents

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Well actually, I AM a president

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: I'm the King of England

jokes.text: Okay, how many times have I told you people the faculty lounge is not a bar?
jokes.setup: Jeff and DeSalvo have been using the faculty lounge as a scotch-fueled conflict arena
jokes.punchline: Frankie's exasperated administrative entrance — 'how many times have I told you people' — treats this as a known, recurring violation
jokes.explanation: Frankie's bureaucratic entrance is a reliable Community joke type — the voice of institutional reason crashing into chaos. 'You people' is funny because it implies this happens regularly. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: No, no, no! That's my briefcase! That one's mine! Stop!

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Come back here! You don't understand, I need that briefcase!

dialogue.speaker: Student 1
dialogue.line: This one's mine!

dialogue.speaker: Student 2
dialogue.line: No, this is clearly mine!

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Nobody move! Nobody's briefcase is leaving this room!

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, WAIT! That's the wrong one!

jokes.text: All right, pack it up people. Come on, you don't have to go teach a class but you can't stay here.
jokes.setup: Frankie clears the faculty lounge
jokes.punchline: The 'you don't have to go home but you can't stay here' riff — modified to 'you don't have to go teach a class' — a pointed reminder that these are teachers who don't teach
jokes.explanation: The 'don't have to go home but can't stay here' subverted to 'don't have to go teach a class' is a solid riff that works on two levels: the bar-closing reference and the specific Greendale faculty joke about not teaching.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's not 'mental,' it's 'mentally challenged.' Get it right.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Oh, my bad. I'll remember that.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You better. And while you're at it, I need you to send me some photos.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Photos? What kind of photos?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Doesn't matter. Just photos. Shirtless. From multiple angles.

jokes.text: Promise no more grifting and promise, if this is worth a million, we'll split it. / You're an idiot. / Or maybe I'm a genius. / No, I can answer that. You're definitely an idiot. / Can an idiot walk backwards like this and not hit anything? / Maybe. Or, maybe not.
jokes.setup: Jeff and DeSalvo propose a truce involving the lottery ticket
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo calls Jeff an idiot; Jeff's comeback is to walk backwards confidently — DeSalvo's 'Maybe. Or, maybe not' implies Jeff immediately hits something
jokes.explanation: Jeff's physical confidence ('can an idiot walk backwards like this?') punctured by DeSalvo's 'Maybe. Or, maybe not' — which implies he immediately fails — is a good visual joke. The flatness of 'Maybe. Or, maybe not' is perfect non-committal deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So either you're incompetent, or you're actively sabotaging me.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: Incompetent.

jokes.text: This guy is a grifter. Professor of grifting. He charges $400, you get two briefcases and your ex-boyfriend becomes an obsessive.
jokes.setup: Britta confronts DeSalvo, apparently having followed Jeff
jokes.punchline: Her summary of DeSalvo's class — '$400, two briefcases, and your ex-boyfriend becomes an obsessive' — frames Jeff's involvement as the real scam victim
jokes.explanation: 'Your ex-boyfriend becomes an obsessive' as a line-item cost of the grifting class is an excellent joke — it reframes Jeff's entire character arc as a service feature (or bug) of DeSalvo's course. The specificity of '$400' and 'two briefcases' sells the deadpan consumer-review tone.

dialogue.speaker: DeSalvo
dialogue.line: I was grifted.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Grift!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Grift!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Grift!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Grift!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Grift!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Grift!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Grift!

jokes.text: I didn't know you and Winger were lovers. If he wanted my respect, he should have opened with that.
jokes.setup: Britta defends Jeff to DeSalvo
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo misreads their relationship as romantic — and says Jeff should have led with that for respect
jokes.explanation: The misread of Jeff and Britta as lovers is a slight callback to Season 1-2 but DeSalvo's reasoning — 'he should have opened with that' — implies having a passionate defender earns credibility in grifter circles. Funny but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: Yeah, so Jeff basically saved my life once, and ever since then he's been... cashing in on it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You owe me, buddy. That's just how this works.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: Do you have any idea how many times you've called in that debt? I've done your laundry, written your papers, covered for you at work...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's what friends do.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: Friends don't systematically exploit a life debt for years, Jeff!

jokes.text: Are you trying to be disarming? Are you grifting me out of my arms?
jokes.setup: DeSalvo asks if Britta is trying to be disarming
jokes.punchline: Britta takes 'disarming' literally — 'grifting me out of my arms' — a defensive, paranoid parsing of a common idiom
jokes.explanation: Wordplay on 'disarming' — Britta now sees all language as potential grift vectors. 'Grifting me out of my arms' is a strange and funny image. The grift paranoia has reached Britta, which tracks.

jokes.text: He took the bait. / Yes. / Wait, I thought we didn't want him to take the bait? / No, no, we're saying the same thing. He didn't take the bait, we didn't want taken. The African Telegram? Yeah, which was offered as fake bait and taken as such, ie, not taken.
jokes.setup: The group tries to debrief on whether DeSalvo took their bait
jokes.punchline: Jeff's explanation becomes recursive nonsense — the more he explains the fake-bait/real-bait distinction, the more confusing it gets, culminating in the group being genuinely confused
jokes.explanation: Jeff confidently explaining a plan that doesn't quite make sense is a layered comedy of incompetence — he sounds authoritative while saying nothing coherent. The confusion is structural: 'we're saying the same thing' followed by an explanation that makes it MORE confusing is excellent.

jokes.text: He can know a plan all he wants. But the plan he knows won't be our plan.
jokes.setup: The group points out DeSalvo knows they're trying to grift him
jokes.punchline: Jeff's confident reassurance — 'the plan he knows won't be our plan' — implies there's a secret plan, but...
jokes.explanation: Jeff delivering a sound-bite of confidence ('the plan he knows won't be our plan') that implies strategic depth while having none — which is revealed immediately after — is a great character-specific joke. High rewatch value because on second viewing you know there is no plan.

jokes.text: Because, oh, my god, Jeff is making this up as we go.
jokes.setup: Jeff's confident 'plan explanation' is becoming increasingly vague
jokes.punchline: Shirley realizes aloud — to the group, in front of Jeff — that he has no plan
jokes.explanation: The 'oh my god' realization mid-scene is a satisfying puncture of Jeff's bravado. The directness of saying it in front of him — 'Jeff is making this up' — without any softening is very funny. High impact because it validates what the audience suspected.

jokes.text: He definitely had a plan in The Sting. / If anybody wants to watch it, it's important you know it knocks out half a calendar day.
jokes.setup: Abed invokes The Sting as a model for how grifts should work
jokes.punchline: His practical warning — 'it knocks out half a calendar day' — frames The Sting as a logistical obstacle rather than a cinematic reference
jokes.explanation: Abed treating The Sting primarily as a time commitment ('half a calendar day') rather than a classic film is a great character-specific joke. It's the kind of hyper-practical cinephile logic only Abed would deploy.

jokes.text: I guess at any of the several dozen points when a normal person would say, by the way, I have no plan.
jokes.setup: Jeff asks why no one called out that he had no plan
jokes.punchline: Annie's answer — 'at any of the several dozen points when a normal person would say, by the way, I have no plan' — is a comprehensive indictment of Jeff's social behavior
jokes.explanation: 'Several dozen points when a normal person would say...' — the qualifier 'several dozen' is funny because it quantifies how many opportunities Jeff had to come clean. Annie's exasperation is calibrated and character-specific.

jokes.text: In The Sting, they do withhold stuff from each other. Or from the audience, but I think for effect. Also, be warned, 20% of the movie is hand drawn.
jokes.setup: Abed continues defending The Sting as a reference model
jokes.punchline: Adding the warning that '20% of the movie is hand drawn' as an important viewer advisory — the kind of detail only Abed would foreground
jokes.explanation: Abed treating '20% hand drawn' as a consumer warning is perfectly him — the kind of precise, slightly irrelevant film fact that he processes as critically important. The deadpan 'be warned' elevation of this detail is great character comedy.

jokes.text: Abed, why don't you marry The Sting? / Okay, just so you know, if I do and we have half Sting children, when they ask me how to grift, I'm gonna tell them to watch their mother, not listen to you!
jokes.setup: Jeff sarcastically tells Abed to marry The Sting
jokes.punchline: Abed takes the hypothetical seriously, constructs a full scenario of 'half Sting children' asking about grifting, and chooses the film (mother) over Jeff as a teaching resource
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Abed engaging fully with the 'marry The Sting' hypothetical — complete with children, custody disputes over teaching methodology, and the film as 'mother' — is an extraordinary piece of character comedy. The specificity of 'half Sting children' asking how to grift is both absurd and logically consistent within Abed's worldview. The final 'not listen to you' is a devastating mic drop that also works as genuine Jeff criticism. High originality, exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Shut up, okay! You guys, you're, you're always picking on me, all right? / Oh. Oh. / And you've really been hammering me lately. / All I had was the idea that, look, look, I, I need this. / I need to be better than this guy.
jokes.setup: Jeff loses his composure after the group calls him out for having no plan
jokes.punchline: Jeff's breakdown reveals his entire motivation is petty ego — he 'needs' to beat DeSalvo — delivered with genuine vulnerability that makes it both funny and sad
jokes.explanation: Jeff's cringe-comedy emotional collapse is a Community staple — the moment where the cool facade drops and pure petty need is exposed. 'I need to be better than this guy' is characteristically Jeff: the honesty is funny, but it also works emotionally. The stammering delivery ('look, look, I, I') adds to the cringe.

jokes.text: Watch The Sting.
jokes.setup: Abed asks what Jeff wants to do with the laptop he brought
jokes.punchline: After his emotional breakdown about needing a plan, Jeff's answer is simply 'Watch The Sting' — he's surrendering to Abed's recommendation
jokes.explanation: Perfect punchline. Jeff's emotional buildup — 'I need this, I need to be better than this guy, let me think' — leads to the most anticlimactic possible answer: watching a movie. Economy score is 10: two words complete a full comedic arc that spans multiple scenes. The irony is that Abed's seemingly irrelevant advocacy paid off. Great structure.

jokes.text: It's over. Whatever. Who got shot? What's going on? Was Sting even in it? That movie was terrible. / You slept the whole time. / Yeah, that's worse. The dialogue seeped into my dreams. My whole brain is long and quiet.
jokes.setup: The group has just watched The Sting and their reactions are all over the place
jokes.punchline: Elroy's 'The dialogue seeped into my dreams. My whole brain is long and quiet.' — a surreal description of absorbing a slow film while sleeping
jokes.explanation: 'My whole brain is long and quiet' is a genuinely original formulation for being bored to sleep. The synaesthetic description of The Sting's pacing as making a brain 'long and quiet' is strange and funny and weirdly evocative. High originality and quotability. The escalating confused reactions ('who got shot? Was Sting even in it?') set up the payoff well.

jokes.text: So how did they grift him? / Well, they basically made a fake building and hired 1,000 people to cooperate in perfect secrecy. / Huh. Should we just do that? / We could watch another grifter movie. / There's more activity in Matchstick Men. / Oh, like what? / At one point they build a fake hospital. / So much construction! / Oh, God, it's so late.
jokes.setup: The group asks what The Sting's grift was
jokes.punchline: The grift requires a fake building and 1,000 people — Jeff's earnest 'Should we just do that?' followed by discovery that Matchstick Men involves a fake hospital — leading to 'So much construction!'
jokes.explanation: 'So much construction!' as the group's unified reaction to movie grifts is delightful — it frames the impossibility of their task through a mundane logistical lens. Jeff's sincere 'Should we just do that?' after hearing about 1,000 actors is also funny. The escalation from one fake building to a whole hospital is well-structured.

jokes.text: You guys are gonna bail on me, aren't you? / I think we have to, Jeff. / We've tried everything we can. Maybe over the weekend I can make a fake building, but all the briefcases, and the swapping, and The Sting? I'm not cut out for it.
jokes.setup: The group is giving up on the grift
jokes.punchline: Annie's consoling speech includes 'Maybe over the weekend I can make a fake building' — a sincere offer to construct a fraudulent skyscraper in 48 hours
jokes.explanation: Annie's earnest 'maybe over the weekend I can make a fake building' is perfect Annie — she's genuinely considering whether she has the bandwidth for a construction project. The sincerity of the offer is what makes it funny. High character integration.

jokes.text: I'm starting to think that real grifts only really happen in the movies, and even in the movies they barely make sense. Look, I'm old. The Sting is terrible. Grifting is stupid. The writing's on the wall.
jokes.setup: The group is demoralized about their inability to execute a real grift
jokes.punchline: Elroy's pragmatic summary dismisses grifts as a movie fiction, then adds 'I'm old' as if that's a coherent argument, then 'The Sting is terrible' as the decisive logic
jokes.explanation: Elroy's sequence of reasoning — real grifts don't happen → I'm old → The Sting is terrible → writing's on the wall — is funny because 'I'm old' and 'The Sting is terrible' are non-sequiturs presented as evidence. Classic Elroy pragmatism.

jokes.text: No, I was wrong. If you remember, I called you a thug. Thugs fight. You're more, nope, I can't think of a metaphor pathetic enough to suit you, Jeff Winger, though I am reminded of something Oscar Wilde once said when he compared sheep to wolves.
jokes.setup: Jeff surrenders and says DeSalvo was right
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo escalates from conceding his insult to constructing an even more elaborate one — culminating in an Oscar Wilde reference he doesn't complete, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: 'I can't think of a metaphor pathetic enough to suit you' is a great insult — it insults Jeff by implying he's beyond the reach of language. The Oscar Wilde name-drop is funny because DeSalvo doesn't finish it, which makes it both a character joke (he's bluffing) and a structural one (the incomplete insult is itself more insulting).

jokes.text: Though I am reminded of something Oscar Wilde once said when he compared sheep to wolves. Screw it.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo appears to quote Oscar Wilde as a final insult.
jokes.punchline: 'Screw it' — he abandons the Wilde quote mid-citation, suggesting even the great Oscar Wilde couldn't muster something pathetic enough.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback to the previous joke — DeSalvo tried Wilde, Wilde failed him too. 'Screw it' as the terminus of a Wilde citation is a funny deflation. The two-word abandonment is very economical.

jokes.text: You hit me with a woman's hand. You Midwestern floozy. / I lived in New York.
jokes.setup: Jeff apparently slaps DeSalvo
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo's insult — 'woman's hand, Midwestern floozy' — provokes Jeff's correction: 'I lived in New York' — as if that's the relevant rebuttal to being called a floozy
jokes.explanation: Jeff not denying 'floozy' but specifically correcting the geography is very funny. 'I lived in New York' implies that makes the slap acceptable, or that New York floozies are of a different, more respected category. The economy of the exchange is tight.

jokes.text: Yeah, right, he's grifting us. / Grift blood. Someone taste it. I'm sure it's Karo Syrup and food dye. / I mean I would, but my diabetes.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo appears to be injured/bleeding after the fight
jokes.punchline: Jeff volunteers the diabetes excuse to avoid tasting the blood — which is an absurd reason but also calls back to the opening diabetes bit
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback. The diabetes joke from the cold open pays off here: Jeff uses his possible diabetes as an excuse to not taste blood, which: (1) proves he actually absorbed Britta's symptoms warning, (2) uses a medical condition as an absurd excuse for cowardice, and (3) suggests he may genuinely have diabetes. 'I mean I would, but my diabetes' has perfect comedic rhythm — the 'my diabetes' is delivered as matter-of-fact ownership of a condition established only as a metaphor at the start. The rewatch bonus is high.

jokes.text: 19, 20, 21. / Are you counting the amount of money or the number of stacks? / [pause] / I have to start over.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo is counting out money; Frankie asks a clarifying question
jokes.punchline: The question makes him lose count, requiring him to start over — slapstick of the mind
jokes.explanation: Classic beat — asking someone counting 'are you counting X or Y' always makes them lose count. The pause before 'I have to start over' is the entire joke and it lands. Not high-concept but well-executed.

jokes.text: I'll do it, move. But I want to go on record as being disgusted by this transaction.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo needs help counting the money; Frankie takes over
jokes.punchline: Frankie helps while simultaneously registering her moral objection — 'on record as being disgusted' — the bureaucratic form of conscience
jokes.explanation: Very Frankie — she participates but files a formal objection. 'I want to go on record' is the language of minutes and proceedings, applied to moral squeamishness. The character integration is high: this is Frankie's entire worldview distilled into one sentence.

jokes.text: Got it. Disgusted.
jokes.setup: Frankie says she wants to go on record as disgusted
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds as if actually maintaining the record — 'Got it. Disgusted.' — treating her objection as a data point
jokes.explanation: Two words do the whole job. 'Got it. Disgusted.' is perfect economy — Jeff plays the secretary to Frankie's objection, treating her moral stand as a transcription exercise. Economy score near-maximum because nothing could be cut.

jokes.text: Me, take a class here? Talk about a rip-off. / Oh! Talk about a ribbing.
jokes.setup: Greendale offers DeSalvo classes as a settlement option; he dismisses them as a rip-off
jokes.punchline: Frankie's 'Talk about a ribbing' — defending Greendale from the man who just ran a grift class there — is a satisfying role reversal
jokes.explanation: Frankie defending Greendale's honor from a professional grifter is a solid institutional loyalty joke. The 'rip-off / ribbing' rhyme is satisfying. Not exceptional but well-placed.

jokes.text: What the hell am I doing? You know, so far, Frankie's disgusted and, that's it. Seems like a waste of a record.
jokes.setup: Jeff watches the settlement go badly
jokes.punchline: Jeff's self-aware commentary on the 'record' — only Frankie's disgust is on it — questioning the value of maintaining it
jokes.explanation: Jeff completing the 'record' callback trilogy — 'seems like a waste of a record' — is tight structural work. He's been ironically maintaining Frankie's objection log and now questions its value. The callback lands because it closes a small three-beat running joke cleanly.

jokes.text: You're a jerk. / You're all jerks. / And this whole school can suck a big one. And you can put that in your record.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo is leaving, insulting everyone
jokes.punchline: 'And you can put that in your record' — DeSalvo appropriates Frankie's bureaucratic formulation as a parting insult, using her procedural language as an exit line
jokes.explanation: DeSalvo hijacking Frankie's bureaucratic register as a parting insult is a satisfying callback. The escalation from professional language to 'this whole school can suck a big one' and back to formal language ('put that in your record') is a good comedic arc.

jokes.text: I'm sorry guys. This is all my fault. / Don't be. I'm the one who got in a pissing match with a jerk. / With a jerk. / You're a jerk. / You're all jerks.
jokes.setup: Jeff apologizes; DeSalvo interrupts to call him a jerk
jokes.punchline: The jerk insult escalates from Jeff (jerk), to group (all jerks), with DeSalvo apparently overhearing Jeff's self-deprecation and deciding everyone qualifies
jokes.explanation: The escalation from one jerk to all jerks is a decent beat but not sharply crafted. Functions as a transitional joke.

jokes.text: Speaking on that topic, Britta, this is all your fault and you're expelled.
jokes.setup: Everyone is apologizing and assigning blame
jokes.punchline: The Dean intervenes to expel Britta — connecting her expulsion to the topic of fault with 'speaking on that topic' as if the logic is obvious
jokes.explanation: The Dean's non-sequitur expulsion, delivered with the logical connector 'speaking on that topic,' is a classic Greendale institutional absurdism. The Dean treating Britta's expulsion as a natural conclusion to the blame discussion is good bureaucratic comedy.

jokes.text: Britta's the heart of this group. She started it as a, as a, as a, as a, as a, as a fake biology group so that she could have sex with Troy.
jokes.setup: Jeff defends Britta against expulsion, calling her 'the heart of this group'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's defense collapses into the actual origin of the study group — Britta invented a fake biology group to pursue Troy romantically — undercutting his flattery
jokes.explanation: Jeff's defense of Britta as 'the heart of this group' collapsing into the reveal that the group was founded on sexual manipulation is a great structural joke. The stammering 'as a, as a, as a' builds anticipation before the deflating truth. The punchline is specific, accurate, and perfectly undercuts the heroic framing. Rewatch bonus for long-time Community fans.

jokes.text: No. That's exactly it. / Oh, okay. Don't let me handle it.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals Britta's founding motivation; Britta is mortified
jokes.punchline: Britta confirms it's exactly right; Jeff's 'Don't let me handle it' is a perfect self-aware exit — he just destroyed her defense and knows it
jokes.explanation: 'Don't let me handle it' is a satisfying self-aware punchline — Jeff acknowledges he made things worse while pretending to help. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: No. You can't expel Britta, she's been here six years. Three more, and she'll have her two-year degree.
jokes.setup: Jeff defends Britta by noting her six years of attendance
jokes.punchline: Three more years for a two-year degree — she's nine years into a two-year program
jokes.explanation: Classic Community joke — the math of Britta's academic career is itself the punchline. 'Three more and she'll have her two-year degree' is efficiently constructed: six years established, then 'three more' implies nine total for a two-year program. Good structure and high character integration.

jokes.text: You can't expel her with four week-isodes left in the seaso-mester. See, it's starting.
jokes.setup: Jeff is building a case to protect Britta from expulsion
jokes.punchline: Abed blends 'episodes/weeks' and 'season/semester' into portmanteaus — 'week-isodes' and 'seaso-mester' — and treats the bleed as a symptom: 'See, it's starting'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the entire episode — possibly Community's entire run. Abed's words bleeding between TV production language and Greendale academic language ('week-isodes,' 'seaso-mester') perfectly captures his character's inability to distinguish fiction from reality. 'See, it's starting' implies he's aware this is a symptom he can't stop. It's meta-commentary, character comedy, and absurdism simultaneously. Near-perfect originality and character integration: this joke could ONLY exist in Community, in this season, delivered by Abed. The portmanteaus are genuinely brilliant coinages.

jokes.text: 50,000. Whoop, I'll just put this in here. Mm-hm. Give it to me. Yep. Don't help me, anyone. Turn me around.
jokes.setup: DeSalvo is settling up with Greendale's $50,000 and needs to exit with the money
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo struggles with the briefcase and exits in an undignified way — 'Don't help me, anyone. Turn me around.' — the grifter revealed as physically incompetent
jokes.explanation: DeSalvo's exit chaos — struggling with money and briefcases and needing to be turned around — is a funny deflation of his confident persona. 'Don't help me, anyone' is a great character line: he insists on dignity while clearly having none.

jokes.text: The plan was to meet later. / So, what's it gonna cost to make you go away? / You know there's a way we could end this very quickly and make a bit of money. / I don't like it, but keep talking. / Yes. That was the plan. / And, your plan was probably to never show up. / Clever girl. Don't trust anyone.
jokes.setup: It's revealed Britta was part of the grift plan all along — she was working with DeSalvo
jokes.punchline: DeSalvo's 'Clever girl. Don't trust anyone.' — the grifter code phrase that closes the reveal, and his admiring recognition of Britta as a natural grifter
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Britta was the inside woman is a satisfying structural payoff. 'Clever girl. Don't trust anyone.' works as both a thematic statement and a character endorsement — DeSalvo, who trusts no one, is impressed. The 'I don't like it, but keep talking' callback implies Britta pitched the grift to DeSalvo and he was reluctantly won over. High rewatch value.

jokes.text: Hang on. Did you have to hit me, for real? / Have to? No. / Now that you're expelled, you might consider a career in grifting. You're quite good at it. / I don't know. How does one go through life like that? / Well, follow me, and I'll show you.
jokes.setup: Post-reveal, Britta asks DeSalvo if he had to hit her for real
jokes.punchline: 'Have to? No.' — DeSalvo chose to hit her; followed by his offer to mentor Britta in grifting, and her philosophical question about grifter life
jokes.explanation: 'Have to? No.' is a great casual admission — he hit her because he could, not because he had to. It's cold and funny. The mentorship offer and 'follow me, and I'll show you' is a solid closing arc beat for Britta's character, though the comedic payoff is lighter.
